paragraphs: This question asks for the average age of Backcourt and Frontcourt players. Both systems create those two groups, but their averages are wrong. QuWARTS reports 30.75 and 27.2 instead of 49.10 and 58.64. DocETL reports 5.68 and 84.76.

QuWARTS found an age for only 36 of 139 player documents, and the reason traces back to how its extraction budget gets divided up. Before extracting anything, QuWARTS looks at every one of the 20 questions in the workload and checks how each column is used: does it ever appear in a GROUP BY or a join, or does it only ever get summed or averaged? Columns used for grouping or joining are pushed toward 75-95% document coverage, because getting those right decides whether the output has the correct rows at all. Columns that are only ever fed into SUM, AVG, or MAX — like age here — are pushed to only about 10%. Once roughly one in ten age cells is filled in, the system considers that column "done" and spends its remaining budget elsewhere, even when plenty of budget is left in the run. Age is never a grouping key anywhere in this workload, so it never earns more than that 10% target.

DocETL extracts one player record per document with its Map operation (§2.2.1 of the paper). The instruction to write -1 for an unknown age is typed directly into that operation's prompt by this benchmark's code — it is a convention used across this benchmark's runners, not something the DocETL paper asks for, and it exists so every extracted record still satisfies the schema's requirement that age be a number. The schema only requires a number, so a wrongly large age satisfies it just as easily as -1 does.

The two problems need different fixes. QuWARTS's age coverage would rise well past 10% if the scheduler treated an averaged column as being as important as a grouping column — that is a scheduling-policy change, not an "extract harder" change. For DocETL, replacing -1 with NULL removes the negative pull; catching an implausible age at all would require a rule that actually judges plausibility, since the schema only checks that the value is a number.

This question counts players by nationality. QuWARTS finds 66 American players instead of 116. DocETL gets closer with 89, but it also creates 11 groups that should not be separate, including Azerbaijan, Nigerian, and even JSON objects stored as nationality names.

Nationality is exactly the kind of column QuWARTS's scheduler is supposed to protect, because it is grouped on here — it should land in the well-funded tier described in q0, not the starved one. The remaining damage comes from a second, separate mechanism: QuWARTS only learns to merge different spellings of the same value ("Dominican" and "Dominican Republic") when the SQL itself hands it a short list of target spellings to learn from, which normally comes from an equality filter like nationality = 'American'. This question has no such filter — it just groups by whatever text shows up — so the system never builds a canonical vocabulary for nationality at all. Every distinct spelling in the source documents becomes its own group, and 116 real Americans get split across however many ways "American" was ever phrased.

DocETL extracts nationality with one Map call per document (§2.2.1 of the paper). This benchmark's harness never calls DocETL's plan optimizer, only its execution engine, so DocETL's Resolve operator — the one piece of the system built specifically to merge near-duplicate values (§2.2.3) — is never constructed for this run. A JSON object converted to text still satisfies the schema's requirement that the field be a string, so it survives unfiltered.

Both systems have a working extraction step and a missing cleanup step. Fixing this needs an actual canonical nationality list to merge against, because neither system's built-in normalization tool turns itself on for a plain GROUP BY with no target values to learn from.

This question joins players to teams and averages each team's NBA championship count. QuWARTS found a team for 84 of its 106 player rows, but a championship count for only 44. A player is also lost from the join whenever the team name on the player row does not exactly match the name in the team table.

The championship count is a textbook case of the pattern from q0: it is never grouped or joined on anywhere in this workload, only averaged, so QuWARTS's scheduler funds it to roughly 10% coverage and stops. What makes this case worth calling out separately is that QuWARTS extracts its player table once and reuses it for every one of the 20 questions — so this same underfunded championship column is not a one-off; it is the identical column limiting q5's MAX, q9's filtered COUNT, and q10's SUM as well. One scheduling decision, made once, ripples through every query that happens to touch that column. The team name, meanwhile, is used to join two tables but is never grouped on in this specific question, so it falls outside the vocabulary-learning mechanism described in q1 too — join-only columns get no canonicalization tool at all, only whatever the raw extraction happened to write down.

DocETL extracts player and team records with separate Map calls (§2.2.1), then joins them by exact text match in SQLite. Several teams end up with an average of exactly -1 because the harness's -1-for-unknown convention (explained in q0) feeds straight into an unfiltered AVG here — nothing in this query's SQL removes it first. The two Map calls also have no shared vocabulary between them, because Resolve and Equijoin (§2.2.3, §2.2.4) are never constructed for this run, so "Bucks" on one side and "Milwaukee Bucks" on the other are just two different strings to SQLite.

The clean way to separate these causes is to fix one thing at a time: swap DocETL's -1 for NULL first, then standardize team names on both sides of the join. For QuWARTS, the fix is upstream of any single query — raising the priority the scheduler assigns to aggregate-only columns would help every query that shares this column, not just this one.

This question keeps only colleges with more than one player, then reports the largest MVP count in each group. QuWARTS returns names such as Duke Blue Devils and Indiana instead of the benchmark's names, and reports 9 for Kentucky instead of 1.

College is grouped on here, but — like nationality in q1 — this query has no equality filter on college, so QuWARTS never gets a target vocabulary to learn from and never merges "Duke University" with "Duke Blue Devils." MVP awards is a pure aggregate column, so it lands in the roughly-10%-coverage tier from q0, which is why only 33 of 106 players have an MVP value at all. The 9 for Kentucky survives a separate step: QuWARTS's plausibility check on raw numeric values only asks "is this an integer," never "is this specifically an MVP count as opposed to some other number in the same passage." That check has no attribute-specific rule to catch a number that's the wrong kind of statistic, only one wide enough to reject nonsense like a fractional or astronomically large value.

DocETL extracts college and MVP count together with one Map call per document (§2.2.1). The -1 convention from q0 is filtered out by the HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 threshold indirectly but not removed from the MVP values themselves, and the same college-spelling problem persists because Resolve is never invoked, for the same reason given in q1.

Two independent checks would separate the causes here: merge college spellings without touching any MVP number, then separately check whether each retained MVP number is actually an MVP count. Fixing spelling alone can produce a clean-looking group that still contains the wrong maximum; fixing the numbers alone can leave the same college split across several names.

This question adds up MVP awards for Backcourt and Frontcourt players. QuWARTS reports 20 and 2021 instead of 14 and 7. DocETL reports -13 and -30. Both systems create the right two groups; the numbers being added are the problem.

MVP awards is aggregate-only, so it is capped at roughly 10% document coverage for the reason explained in q0 — only 30.9% is actually a little above that floor, but coverage stopping this early is still why so few real awards ever get summed. The 2009 that leaked into the Frontcourt total, and the Stephen Curry row that stores seven MVPs instead of two, are both the same type-only plausibility gap from q3: nothing in QuWARTS checks that a number labeled "MVP awards" is actually counting MVP awards rather than a nearby draft year or some other statistic in the same passage.

DocETL's -1 convention, explained in q0, interacts differently with different SQL depending on which aggregate consumes it. A filtered AVG or MAX can simply exclude -1 before it does any damage — that is what happens in several other questions in this set. An unfiltered SUM has no such protection: every player without a known MVP count subtracts exactly one from the total, which is why DocETL's totals land at -13 and -30 instead of near zero. The harm from one fixed placeholder convention, in other words, depends entirely on which arithmetic operation is downstream of it, not on how good the extraction was.

Converting -1 to NULL removes DocETL's negative-total problem outright, because it is purely an artifact of that convention meeting an unguarded SUM. QuWARTS's errors are not sentinel arithmetic at all — rejecting the year-sized 2009 only gets Frontcourt from 2021 to 12, and Curry's seven-to-two mistake still needs to be checked against its source passage directly.

This question finds the largest NBA championship count for each nationality. QuWARTS is slightly closer overall. It returns seven nationality groups, but uses Dominican Republic instead of Dominican and Nigerian instead of Nigerian-American, and reports two championships for British players instead of one. DocETL returns six groups, misses British and Congolese, and adds Croatian.

This is the same championship column that q2 traced back to QuWARTS's single shared extraction pass — nba_championships is only ever aggregated across this workload, so it was funded to roughly 10% coverage once and never revisited. The Stephen Curry row is the clearest single failure: QuWARTS correctly identifies him from Davidson, draft pick seven, 2009, and Golden State, but stores seven NBA championships instead of four, and because this query takes a MAX, that one wrong number becomes the entire answer for American players. Nationality's alias problem is the same vocabulary gap from q1: this query groups by nationality with no equality filter, so QuWARTS never learns which spellings should be merged.

DocETL's -1 convention does no damage here, for the reason given in q4: the SQL filters out anything below 1 before taking the MAX, so the placeholder is filtered away before it can distort the result. What is left is a mix of missing facts, wrong championship counts, and nationality spellings that don't match the benchmark — the same alias gap as QuWARTS, arrived at by a different route, since DocETL never constructs a Resolve step either.

There's also a genuine benchmark-answer defect here: the American gold value is an empty string despite the query requiring a positive maximum, and that should be corrected before either system is scored on it. After that, nationality spelling and championship-value correctness are two separate problems that need two separate tests.

This question counts players drafted in each year after 2010. QuWARTS returns every year from 2011 through 2023 and gets many counts right. DocETL returns 12 of the 13 years, missing 2022, and some counts are wrong — for example, it reports seven players in 2011 instead of three.

Draft year is unusual in this workload: it is grouped on directly (counted per year), so it earns QuWARTS's higher coverage tier the way nationality or college would if this question had filtered on them — which is consistent with why QuWARTS's structure holds up well here even with only 56.8% of documents actually having a draft year. But draft year is also a number, and QuWARTS's vocabulary-learning mechanism (the one described in q1) only ever applies to text columns — it has no equivalent for teaching the system what a plausible draft year looks like. So a column that got the generous coverage budget still has no defense against a nearby season year or article year being mistaken for the draft year, because the only check left is "is this an integer," the same type-only gap from q3.

DocETL extracts draft year with one Map call per document (§2.2.1). The filter draft_year > 2010 happens to remove the -1 placeholder from q0 automatically, so the sentinel isn't the problem here. What remains is the same generic gap as QuWARTS: the schema only declares this field as a number, with no instruction distinguishing "the year this player was drafted" from any other year mentioned nearby.

The benchmark answer itself has an empty-string year group despite the SQL requiring draft_year > 2010, which should be removed first. After that, the real test is row-level: compare each saved draft year against its source passage and retry only the ones that don't hold up, rather than rerunning the whole aggregate query and hoping the count moves in the right direction.

This question finds the smallest draft pick among players on each current team. It needs three things to line up: the player's team, the draft pick, and an exact match to the team table's name. QuWARTS misses several benchmark teams and adds Memphis. It reports 3 for Boston instead of 1 and 8 for Milwaukee instead of 1.

Team is used as both a join key and, elsewhere in this workload, a grouping key, so it lands in QuWARTS's better-funded coverage tier — 84 of 106 rows have some team value. But there's a second gap this question exposes that hasn't come up yet: QuWARTS's underlying data model has no notion of "as of when." A team name that was once true for a player is stored the same way a currently-true one is, with no timestamp attached, so a stale-but-real team assignment passes every check the system has. That is a schema-design gap, not a coverage gap — more budget spent extracting team names would not fix it, because the system has nowhere to record which one is current.

DocETL extracts player and team as two independent Map calls (§2.2.1) with no shared vocabulary between them, for the same reason given in q2 — Resolve and Equijoin are never constructed for this benchmark run. DocETL's schema has exactly the same blind spot as QuWARTS on the temporal question: nothing in its output format represents "current team" versus "any team this player has ever been on." This is a modeling gap shared by both systems, not something either extraction pipeline happens to handle better.

Two separate fixes are needed, and neither is really about extraction quality: give every franchise one stable identifier so spelling differences stop breaking joins, and add an explicit "as of" field to the player-team relationship in both systems' schemas so a stale assignment can actually be recognized as stale.

This question averages Olympic gold medals for Backcourt and Frontcourt players who have at least one medal. QuWARTS reports 1.92 and 1.38 instead of 1.44 and 1.57. DocETL reports 2.33 and 1.0. Both systems create the right two position groups, but neither gets both averages close enough.

Position is the group-by column here, and it is fully correct — which is exactly what q0's scheduling policy predicts, since group-by columns get the well-funded coverage tier. Olympic gold medals is purely aggregated, so it gets the roughly-10% tier instead, landing at 23% coverage. The same Stephen Curry row that stored the wrong championship count in q5 and the wrong MVP count in q4 also stores six Olympic golds instead of one — by now a pattern rather than a coincidence: one player's extraction record has multiple wrong achievement counts, all passing the same type-only check because none of QuWARTS's raw-route validation is specific to what "Olympic gold medals" should look like versus any other small integer in that player's biography.

DocETL's -1 convention does no harm here either, for the same reason as q5: the query filters for at least one medal before averaging, which removes -1 automatically. What's left is the same generic numeric-typing gap described throughout this set — the schema asks for a number, not specifically an Olympic medal count.

The cleanest test freezes the position groups, which are already right, and audits only the medal numbers within them — recomputing the averages using only values that survive a plausibility check would show directly how much of the gap comes from a handful of wrong positive numbers versus real missing data.

This question counts NBA champions by college, filtered to players with at least one championship. QuWARTS uses names such as Davidson College, Duke Blue Devils, California Golden Bears, and Indiana, so many benchmark groups appear missing even when the underlying player was found correctly.

This question combines two gaps that have each shown up separately already: college is grouped on with no equality filter, so it falls into the same unmerged-vocabulary trap as q1 and q3, and nba_championships is aggregate-only, so it is capped near the 10% coverage tier from q0. Because both weaknesses hit the same query at once, the effect compounds — a player can be correctly found, correctly attributed a real championship, and still vanish from the count because their college string doesn't match any of the benchmark's spellings.

DocETL extracts both fields with one Map call (§2.2.1). The -1 placeholder is removed by this query's >=1 filter, so it isn't the active problem here, but college spelling is unmerged for the identical reason as QuWARTS: no Resolve step is ever constructed for this benchmark run.

Because two independent problems are stacked here, they need two independent tests: standardize college names while leaving championship values untouched, and separately verify that each retained positive championship count is real. Either fix alone will look like partial progress; only doing both explains the full gap.

This question adds up FIBA World Cup titles by team. Some results are obviously not title counts: QuWARTS reports 1986 for Indiana, while DocETL reports 50 for Bucks and 57 for Cleveland. The SQL is adding correctly; the wrong numbers were already in the tables before the SQL ran.

FIBA World Cup titles is the most extreme case of the pattern first described in q0: it is never grouped or joined on anywhere in this workload, so it gets the same roughly-10% coverage target as every other pure aggregate column, and here that translates to only 18.7% actual coverage — the sparsest of any measure in this set. The 1986 that ends up in Indiana's total is the same type-only gap from q3 and q4 playing out with an unusually clean example: a calendar year is a perfectly ordinary integer, and QuWARTS's raw-route check has no rule that says a title count should look nothing like a year.

DocETL's Map schema for this field is likewise just "a number" (§2.2.1), so 50 and 57 pass the same way 1986 does on the QuWARTS side — this benchmark's numeric schemas never carry a plausible-range hint for any attribute, on either system. Neither Resolve nor Equijoin would turn a wrong title count into a right one even if they were used, since the number itself, not the join, is what's broken.

There is also a genuine flaw in the benchmark answer: it includes Los Angeles Clippers=0 even though the SQL requires at least one title, because a blank string was treated as a number and summed to zero rather than excluded. That should become NULL before either system is judged on this cell. Beyond that fix, both systems need a rule that actually distinguishes a title count from any other small number a biography happens to mention.

This question counts players aged 20 to 40 by nationality. DocETL finds 45 American players, close to the benchmark's 49. QuWARTS finds only 24 and returns eight of the 17 expected nationality groups.

This question needs two columns to both be right, and both happen to be the weak kind described earlier in this set: age is aggregate/filter-only, so it is capped near the 10% coverage tier from q0 (actual coverage: 25.9%), and nationality is grouped with no equality filter, so it never gets a canonical vocabulary for the reason given in q1. Losing either field removes a player from the count, so the two gaps compound the same way they did in q9.

DocETL's -1 age placeholder is filtered out automatically by the BETWEEN 20 AND 40 condition, matching the pattern from q5 and q8 where a filtered comparison neutralizes the sentinel. What's left is the nationality-alias problem shared with QuWARTS, plus a genuinely time-sensitive detail neither system's schema handles: a biography can correctly state an age that was true when it was written but is no longer true by the benchmark's reference date, and nothing in either system's data model records when a stated age was true.

Retrying only the missing age and nationality cells would test how much of this gap is coverage versus alias drift. The more durable fix for both systems is to store a birth date and compute age against a stated reference date, so a textually correct but outdated age stops being indistinguishable from a current one.

This question finds the largest championship total for each city. QuWARTS returns 29 rows, the same count as the benchmark, and scores better than DocETL. But 12 expected city names are missing and 12 unexpected names appear instead — many are different descriptions of the same place, such as Brooklyn versus "New York City borough of Brooklyn."

Location is grouped on here, so it lands in QuWARTS's well-funded coverage tier — 93.5% of team documents have some location value, which is why the row count matches the benchmark exactly. But this question groups by city with no equality filter on it, so it falls into the same unmerged-vocabulary gap as college in q3 and q9: presence is solid, spelling consistency is not. Championship total is aggregate-only, landing at 71% coverage — better than the extreme case in q10, simply because this particular workload happened to route more of its overall budget toward the team relation, but the underlying policy is identical. The values that did get extracted still pass through the same type-only gate, which is how 1995 and 1978 end up stored as championship counts.

DocETL extracts one record per team with a single Map call (§2.2.1), yet only 20 city groups survive — fewer than QuWARTS despite the "one record per document" design. It uses -1 for unknown titles and also produces clearly wrong values like Cleveland=23 and Toronto=59, both instances of the same generic numeric-typing gap seen throughout this set.

The changes should be tested one at a time: standardize current city names first, then remove year-sized championship values, then retry the cells that are still missing. Bundling them into one rerun would hide which of the two independent gaps — spelling or magnitude — actually explains the improvement.
This question counts teams founded before 1970 in each city. DocETL returns 16 city groups and is much closer to the benchmark than QuWARTS, which returns only seven.

Founded year is used only as a filter in this question — the grouping column is city, not founded year — so founded year itself falls into the roughly-10% coverage tier from q0 rather than city's better-funded tier, which is why only 58.1% of team rows have a founding year at all. City has the same unmerged-spelling gap described in q12: Manhattan and "New York City borough of Brooklyn" are treated as separate places because nothing taught the system they should merge.

DocETL's -1 convention produces its sharpest effect yet here, and it's worth stating plainly why: earlier questions showed that a filter like >=1 or a range like BETWEEN safely removes -1 before it can do damage. A less-than filter does the opposite — since -1 is less than 1970, every player with an unknown founding year incorrectly passes the filter as if their team were historic. Some of DocETL's 16 groups are therefore real matches and some are sentinel artifacts, and the two can't be told apart without inspecting the underlying rows.

The first rerun should replace -1 with NULL, which would show exactly how many of DocETL's 16 groups survive on real data rather than a placeholder. Then city names should be standardized on both systems, and QuWARTS can separately retry the founding years it's missing to recover teams that were excluded only because the year was absent, not because they don't qualify.

This question adds team championships by owner. Both systems score very poorly, but part of the problem is the benchmark itself: before running the reference SQL, the benchmark silently replaces owner names from the team table with names from a separate owner table that neither system is given. A document may say "Dan Gilbert," yet the answer expects "Daniel Gilbert."

Independent of that benchmark defect, owner is grouped on here with no equality filter, so it falls into the same unmerged-vocabulary gap described in q1, q3, q9, and q12 — QuWARTS never builds a canonical owner list because the SQL never hands it one. Championship values inherit the same type-only numeric gap from q10, which is how 1995 and 1978 end up counted as championships.

DocETL extracts only from each team document with one Map call (§2.2.1), so it has no access to the separate owner table either — and even if it did, no Resolve step exists in this run to reconcile the two tables' spellings, for the same reason given throughout this set. No amount of per-document extraction quality can recover a scoring rule that was never disclosed to either system.

The benchmark needs to be fixed before the systems can be compared fairly here: either score the owner names exactly as they appear in the team data, or give both systems the owner table and the rule for using it. Only after that is resolved do the recurring owner-alias and championship-value problems become measurable on their own terms.

This question averages championships by city after removing missing and negative values. QuWARTS scores slightly better and gets many city averages exactly right. DocETL returns slightly more of the expected cities, but it also includes old franchise locations such as Kansas City, New Jersey, and Minneapolis.

City's spelling problem here is the same unmerged-vocabulary gap from q12 and q13, and championship's wrong values are the same type-only numeric gap from q10 and q14 — by this point in the workload, those two mechanisms account for nearly every remaining QuWARTS error in this question.

DocETL's old franchise cities point at a gap that's different from anything covered so far: it isn't a spelling problem or a sentinel problem, it's that DocETL's extracted records, like QuWARTS's, have no concept of when a city was a team's home versus when it used to be. "New Jersey" and "Minneapolis" may be perfectly accurate facts about the past, extracted correctly, and still wrong for a question asking about the present. This is the same temporal-modeling gap identified in q7, showing up again in a different relation.

A schema fix, not an extraction fix, is what actually closes this gap: represent each team fact as franchise, location, championship total, and the span of years the location was valid, on both systems. A smaller test could correct only city spellings while leaving championship values untouched, then do the reverse, to see which of the two now-familiar problems is doing more damage in this particular question.

This question averages team-owner ages by nationality. QuWARTS reports 67.2 for American owners, reasonably close to 72.14. DocETL reports 289.07 for American owners and -1 for Canadian owners. Neither of those DocETL numbers is an averaging mistake — they come directly from bad input values.

Owner age is aggregate-only, so it gets the same roughly-10% coverage policy from q0 — but here it plays out on a different relation than age did in q0, which is worth noting explicitly: this isn't a fluke specific to player ages, it's QuWARTS's general policy toward any column used only inside an average, regardless of which table it lives in. That policy produced only five owner rows with an age at all. Nationality's Taiwanese-Canadian versus Canadian mismatch is the same unmerged-vocabulary gap from q1, q9, and q11.

DocETL's -1 and 289 both satisfy the same generic "return a number" schema requirement described in q0 and q10 — nothing in this benchmark's schemas has ever included a plausible-age range, for owners any more than for players.

Converting -1 to NULL and rejecting impossible ages would remove the worst distortions immediately, but both systems would still be missing most owners. The durable fix, as in q11, is to extract a birth date and compute age against a declared reference date, so age stops being a raw number with no way to check it.

This question finds the earliest team-acquisition year since 2000 for each owner nationality. DocETL gets the American answer exactly right at 2000. QuWARTS reports 2005. Both systems miss the Taiwanese-Canadian group, whose correct answer is 2019.

QuWARTS actually attempted extraction on almost every owner document — 90.9% coverage — which makes this a useful counterexample to the pattern in earlier questions: more attempts do not automatically produce the correct value. The scheduler's coverage floors control how many documents get tried, not whether the one document containing the true 2000 acquisition ever produced a usable extraction. Since this query takes a MIN, a single missing correct value directly changes the answer to whatever the next-best surviving value happens to be — 2005 here — the same way a single wrong value directly changes a MAX in q5 or q10.

DocETL's per-document Map extraction (§2.2.1) happens to succeed on the American minimum but never recovers a second nationality's acquisition year at all, and there is no retry step in this run to revisit a document that failed the first time — the same absence of a repair pass described for QuWARTS elsewhere in this set, just realized differently since DocETL doesn't share a database across queries the way QuWARTS does.

Checking each saved owner-year pair against its source passage, rather than only looking at the final MIN, would show whether the missing 2000 value was never extracted or was extracted and then discarded. The Taiwanese-Canadian naming issue should be tested separately, so a labeling problem doesn't get confused with a missing acquisition year.

This question averages city populations by state. It is one of QuWARTS's best results: all expected state groups are present, and its score at the 20% error threshold is 0.955. QuWARTS found population in 82.9% of city documents and state in 80%.

This question is worth reading as the positive control for everything explained in q0: population and state both happen to be well-represented in this workload's roles, so they land in QuWARTS's better-funded coverage tier rather than the roughly-10% one, and that is exactly why presence is nearly complete here. What's left is a gap this set hasn't named yet: QuWARTS's data model has no field for what a number means or which year it describes, only a bare numeric value. That's why New York's 92,824 — the number of homeless people in the city's shelter system — gets used as if it were the city's population, and why Phoenix and Salt Lake City each keep an older census figure instead of the source's more recent one. Coverage isn't the problem in this question; the model's inability to represent "population, as of this year" is.

DocETL extracts population and state with one Map call (§2.2.1), and the same -1 convention from q0 feeds directly into this query's AVG the way it did in q2 and q4: Florida's average becomes 221,120 because one city's real value is averaged against a literal -1 rather than against a missing entry. DocETL's schema has exactly the same blind spot as QuWARTS on what a number means or when it was true.

Replacing -1 with NULL fixes DocETL's placeholder arithmetic outright. The value-selection mistakes on both systems need a different fix: storing what each number measures and the year it describes, so a homelessness count or an outdated census figure stops being indistinguishable from a current population.

This question finds the largest GDP among cities with more than one million people, grouped by state. QuWARTS returns six of the seven states but none of its values are close enough. Arizona is 362,000,000,000 while the benchmark stores 362,000. Pennsylvania is 518,500,000,000 while the benchmark stores 518.5. DocETL returns five states, mostly with -1.

GDP is aggregate-only, so it gets the roughly-10% coverage policy from q0 (actual coverage: 31.4%). But the scale mismatch is a different and arguably more interesting gap: QuWARTS's column-type system recognizes integer, real, text, and boolean, and nothing else — there is no unit-of-measure or scale field anywhere in it. A trillion-dollar figure and a million-dollar figure are both just "a real number" to the plausibility check, so nothing in the system can tell that 362,000,000,000 and 362,000 disagree by six orders of magnitude. This question also shows how one bad cell reaches further than its own query: New York is missing here for the same reason it had the wrong number in q18 — its population was extracted as 92,824, so it fails this question's population > 1,000,000 filter too, the same shared-extraction ripple effect first described in q2.

DocETL's Map schema asks for GDP as a plain number (§2.2.1) and writes -1 when it's unknown, the same convention as every other numeric field in this benchmark. Like QuWARTS, DocETL's output format has no place to record currency, scale, reference year, or whether a figure describes a city versus its wider metro area — this is a gap both systems share, not one that happens to affect only one of them.

GDP needs to be represented with its scale, currency, and reference year on both systems, with the benchmark's own values converted to a matching convention before comparison. Population eligibility is a separate problem: fixing GDP's units will not bring back a city that a different query's population mistake already excluded.
